Dendritic cells have many of the markers of macrophages, but they have an additional function. They are able to migrate from the site of infection via lymphatic vessels and present T naïve T cells with MHC/peptide complexes. In a normal dose of paracetamol, it is metabolized by UGT enzymes, then in the liver, into water soluble metabolites which are then excreted from the body via the kidneys.  However, in a toxic dose, some of the paracetamol is metabolized by cytochrome P450 enzymes (specifically CYP2E1) into a toxic intermediate which is then converted into NAPBQII by further CYP450 enzymes.  This NAPBQII is highly toxic as it covalently binds to hepatic glutathione, causing hepatocyte necrosis.  To manage a paracetamol overdose, the mucolide drug n-acetylcysteine (NAC) is given.  NAC has a very similar structure to hepatic glutathione and works by restoring glutathione levels in hepatocytes which reduces the hepatotoxicity of NAPBQII.  It also acts as an alternative rate of clearance of NAPBQII by conjugation.

CFTR is a Cl- channel found on the apical surface of many epithelial cells. It allows Cl- to be secreted/exit cells. It is regulated by 2nd messenger cAMP (increases PTM of CFTR) and sodium (causes apical Cl- to create a negative charge, causing more Na+ into cells to maintain electroneutrality). NaCl cotransporters also help to regulate the activity of CFTR by providing the electrochemical gradient for Cl- secretion.  In the airways, Cl- secretion causes a negative charge, into which water is drawn via aquaporins. This creates a hypertonic layer on the surface of the epithelium, which helps to keep the mucus layer in place. In sweat glands, Cl- secretion draws out Na+ (hence the name "sweat salt")

C is the correct answer.  In the PCT, Na+ is absorbed along with glucose via the symporter. This creates a glucose sensing mechanism as if there is too much glucose in the blood, the PCT will be 'saturated' and less Na+ will be absorbed.  In the thick ascending limb, the ion pump is impermeable to water so as the K+ and Cl- move into the cells, the filtrate becomes positively charged. This creates a potential that pulls Na+ out of the limb into the glomerulus, where it can be reabsorbed in the PCT.  In the DCT, the mechanism is similar to the PCT, with the exception that it uses the NKCC1 instead of the SLC (Na+/glucose) transporter.

Hypoxaemia --> Type 2 respiratory failure --> hypoventilation --> hypercapnia (high PaCO2) --> respiratory acidosis  as a result of PaCO2 being a non-volatile acid that tends to dissociate in the blood and cause acidosis.  The compensation is metabolic, where the increase in HCO3- drives the pH back to normal.  The fact that the pH is normal tells us that the system is compensated.  The fact that the Pa O2 is high enough to not be considered hypoxaemic (on 40% O2, N >10 on air) suggests that this patient is in a chronic state of hypercapnia, where compensation has time to occur.
